Lol. Completely agreed except the chicken part. It definitely tastes like something that was drug through a swamp though.
That nasty, swampy flavor (typically, that smell is produced by algae) probably has a lot to do with what the gator was eating and how it was raised. Gator drinking hard liquor, eating chips and soda while watching Family Feud for 4 hours a day will probably taste different than a gator eating organic fish,doing yoga, and drinking 8 cups of smart water a day. The restaurant we ate at in NW Florida (forgot the name, but I was the only Asian-ish dude there....fortunately, Axel and Damon helped me blend in) was packed full of people, the chefs probably had a lot to do with making it taste good. I've had wild catfish BBQ'ed that tasted amazing, but also had farm raised catfish that tasted like the smell of nasty, swampy freshwater that has been marinating in rotting algae extract for a while.




Very true Mike, although the one time I tried it was a "high dollar seafood restaurant" in the Orlando area (unfortunately old age has stricken my memory as well, and I can't remember the name). It was like 15 bucks for 10 gator tail bites. I probably should've noted I don't like seafood to begin with and since we were with a banquet they offered two appetizers, some kind of fish and I hope these gator bites don't taste like fish. Being they were probably fried in the same oil as the rest of the seafood there that probably skewed my taste for it too. Although it didn't really taste too fishy.

I imagine the original plant is now gone in the wild, like most of that areas Sarr's. I have a few seedlings kicking around from self'd flowers, but they aren't any more vigorous than the parent pictured. Seems like when you get to extreme whites, growth is slower. Throwing some pale leuco genes in should help. I'd like to see what happens if it were crossed with a black-red alata or Bubba, which can get a white top dusting.

We had a psittacina pop up from seed which was all white and pink/red veins, no visible green. I was hoping the plant was masking chlorophyll, but, alas, it was free of chlorophyll and died after using up what nutrients were in the seed.

posts.body_html:
Now that I've been to this site many times over almost a 2 decade period of time, it makes me realize the following:
1) despite no signs of recent burning, the site still looks decently healthy! yes, it's getting really thick in there, but the plants are still surviving. It has always been very heavy with thick grass and a little bit of shrub growth, but for whatever reason, the site stays relatively open, so the plants survive.
2) Production of pitchers during the fall (ie. seeing a lot of them versus not seeing much) isn't a good measure of how well the population is doing overall, it's a good indication of how the plants are doing that year. At this site, I saw the plants looking really dismal, and then 2 years later the field was filled with nice looking pitchers everywhere!
3) If you judged the health of this site by seeing the fall pitchers this year, you'd probably think this site is in steep decline because there were barely any fall pitchers this year. On the contrary, the site is still loaded with plants, but most of them didn't perform for whatever reason. It's also still in full sun and aside from thick grass and less pitchers, it looks the same as it did almost 20 years ago.

Had the trees or brush become thicker at this site, then I'd think this site is in danger, but in the long haul, it seems to be doing alright. But it's still pretty open, and if it got burned, I bet the site would be loaded with lots of pitcher production given a good grow year.

All that aside, here are some 2018 shots from the site:








S. rosea either is or was historically not too far away from this site:



Look at this areolata hybrid and notice the amazing colors:



heat stress causes fall flowering (to pre-empt any scientists, this is just an observation, not a scientific discovery )













If S. psittacina can survive at this site, that's a good sign that the site is suitable for Sarracenias in general:
